claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations and domain-level heterogeneity.
A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate can accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate will use measured domain size, interfacial density, and chemical-fluctuation intensity as input descriptors.
TEM/EDS can provide the microstructural descriptors needed by the proposed surrogate.
The surrogate will embed physical constraints derived from sources such as interatomic potentials.
The model will be calibrated using room-temperature tensile tests at strain rates near 10^-3 s^-1.
Domain size, interfacial density, and fluctuation amplitude serve as proxies for underlying chemical and structural inhomogeneities.
Embedding physical constraints limits model predictions to physically realistic regimes.
Measured microstructural descriptors capture local variations that mediate macroscopic mechanical properties.
An uncertainty-quantification module will flag predictions when input-data quality is low.
Uncertainty flagging ensures that only reliable predictions are made.
The surrogate will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness with errors of approximately ±7–10%.
The surrogate will achieve computational-efficiency gains of at least 50% over full-scale CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.
High-fidelity physically based property calculations are computationally demanding relative to machine-learning surrogates.
Existing computational methods have relatively high uncertainty, particularly for toughness prediction.
The surrogate may become unreliable when descriptors are noisy, unrepresentative, or drawn from a heterostructure substantially different from the calibration state.
Loading conditions or strain rates outside the calibration range may invalidate the predictions.
A blinded prospective benchmark will compare predictions against independently measured tensile and fracture properties of separately prepared HfNbTiVAl10 specimens.
The hypothesis is falsified if the mean prediction error for any target property consistently exceeds 10% under calibration-matched conditions.
